prompt: What is a buffer?

choices.text: A solution that resists dramatic changes in pH
A solution that always has a pH of exactly 7
choices.why: Buffers can have many pH values; what matters is that they resist changes in pH.

choices.text: A strong acid that neutralizes bases
choices.why: Buffers are made from weak acids or weak bases and their salts, not strong acids.

choices.text: A substance that changes color with pH
choices.why: That is an indicator.

explanation: A buffer is a solution that resists dramatic changes in pH.

prompt: What pairs of solutes make up a buffer?

choices.text: A weak acid plus a salt derived from that weak acid, or a weak base plus a salt of that weak base
A strong acid plus a strong base
choices.why: These neutralize each other completely. Buffers need a weak acid or weak base with its salt.

choices.text: A strong acid plus its salt
choices.why: A strong acid is 100% ionized, so its anion won't take up added H^+. Buffers use weak acids.

choices.text: Any acid plus any salt
choices.why: The salt must derive from the same weak acid (or weak base), so the two can trade protons.

explanation: Buffers are composed of certain pairs of solutes: either a weak acid plus a salt derived from that weak acid, or a weak base plus a salt of that weak base.

prompt: Which combination of solutes can make a buffer?

choices.text: HF and NaF
HNO3 and NaNO3
choices.why: HNO3 is a strong acid, so this combination can't make a buffer.

choices.text: HF and NaCl
choices.why: NaCl isn't a salt of HF. The salt must come from the same weak acid: NaF.

choices.text: NaOH and NaF
choices.why: NaOH is a strong base. A buffer needs a weak acid with its salt, or a weak base with its salt.

explanation: HF is a weak acid, and NaF is a salt derived from it (it contains F^−, the anion of HF). Together they make a buffer.

prompt: Which combination of solutes can make a buffer?

choices.text: NH3 and NH4NO3
KOH and KNO3
choices.why: KOH is a strong base. A buffer needs a weak base and a salt of that weak base.

choices.text: NH4Cl and NaCl
choices.why: There's no weak base here; NH4Cl needs to be paired with NH3 itself.

choices.text: HNO3 and NH4NO3
choices.why: HNO3 is a strong acid. The weak base NH3 is missing.

explanation: NH3 is a weak base, and NH4NO3 contains NH4^+, a salt derived from that weak base. Together they make a buffer.

prompt: A student proposes making a buffer from HBr and NaBr, an acid and its salt. Why won't this work?

choices.text: HBr is a strong acid; a buffer needs a weak acid.
NaBr isn't a salt of HBr.
choices.why: NaBr does contain Br^−, the anion of HBr. The problem is that HBr is strong.

choices.text: Buffers can only be made from bases.
choices.why: Buffers can be made from a weak acid and its salt too, like HC2H3O2 and NaC2H3O2.

choices.text: It will work; any acid with its salt is a buffer.
choices.why: Only a weak acid with its salt works. Br^− from a strong acid won't take up added H^+.

explanation: HBr is a strong acid, not a weak acid, so HBr and NaBr can't make a buffer. A buffer needs a weak acid plus a salt of that weak acid (or a weak base plus its salt).

prompt: A student tries to make a buffer from acetic acid, HC2H3O2, and sodium chloride, NaCl. Why won't this work?

choices.text: The salt must derive from the same weak acid, such as NaC2H3O2; NaCl doesn't.
Acetic acid is a strong acid.
choices.why: Acetic acid is a weak acid, which is fine. The problem is the salt.

choices.text: NaCl is a base.
choices.why: NaCl is a neutral salt. It just doesn't supply the acetate ion the buffer needs.

choices.text: It will work; any weak acid with any salt is a buffer.
choices.why: The salt must contain the anion of that weak acid, so it can take up added H^+.

explanation: A buffer needs a weak acid plus a salt derived from that weak acid. HC2H3O2 needs an acetate salt such as NaC2H3O2, whose C2H3O2^− ions can react with added H^+.

prompt: A strong base, a source of OH^− ions, is added to an HC2H3O2/NaC2H3O2 buffer. What happens to the added OH^−?

choices.text: It reacts with HC2H3O2: HC2H3O2 + OH^− → H2O + C2H3O2^−
It reacts with C2H3O2^−, making the solution more basic.
choices.why: C2H3O2^− is the base part of the buffer; it takes up added H^+, not OH^−.

choices.text: It stays in solution and raises the pH sharply.
choices.why: The buffer's weak acid reacts with the OH^− to make water, so the pH doesn't change much.

choices.text: It reacts with Na^+ to form NaOH.
choices.why: Na^+ is a spectator ion. The HC2H3O2 neutralizes the added OH^−.

explanation: Added OH^− ions react with HC2H3O2 in an acid-base reaction, making H2O and C2H3O2^−. Rather than making the solution basic, the OH^− is used up, so the pH doesn't change much.

prompt: A strong acid, a source of H^+ ions, is added to an HC2H3O2/NaC2H3O2 buffer. What happens to the added H^+?

choices.text: It reacts with C2H3O2^− to make molecules of the weak acid HC2H3O2.
It reacts with HC2H3O2, making a stronger acid.
choices.why: HC2H3O2 is the acid part; it neutralizes added OH^−. Added H^+ combines with the acetate ion.

choices.text: It stays in solution and lowers the pH sharply.
choices.why: Because HC2H3O2 is a weak acid, H^+ and C2H3O2^− come together to form it, so the pH doesn't change much.

choices.text: It reacts with Na^+.
choices.why: Na^+ is a spectator ion. The acetate ion takes up the H^+.

explanation: Because HC2H3O2 is a weak acid, H^+ and C2H3O2^− ions in the same solution come together to make HC2H3O2: H^+ + C2H3O2^− → HC2H3O2. The added H^+ is tied up in weak acid molecules.

prompt: In a buffer of NH3 and NH4Cl, which species reacts with added H^+ ions?

choices.text: NH3, forming NH4^+
NH4^+
choices.why: NH4^+ is the acid part of the buffer; it reacts with added OH^−, not H^+.

choices.text: Cl^−, forming HCl
choices.why: Cl^− comes from a strong acid and doesn't take up H^+. NH3, the weak base, does.

choices.text: Nothing; NH3 buffers react only with OH^−
choices.why: The NH3 molecules react with added H^+: NH3 + H^+ → NH4^+.

explanation: In an NH3/NH4Cl buffer, NH3 molecules react with excess H^+ ions introduced by strong acids: NH3(aq) + H^+(aq) → NH4^+(aq).

prompt: In a buffer of NH3 and NH4Cl, which species reacts with added OH^− ions?

choices.text: NH4^+, forming NH3 and H2O
NH3, forming NH2^− and H2O
choices.why: NH3 is the base part of the buffer; it takes up added H^+. NH4^+ neutralizes OH^−.

choices.text: Cl^−, forming HOCl
choices.why: Cl^− doesn't react with OH^−. The ammonium ion does.

choices.text: Nothing; the OH^− stays in solution
choices.why: NH4^+ reacts with it: NH4^+ + OH^− → NH3 + H2O.

explanation: The ammonium ion reacts with hydroxide ions introduced by strong bases: NH4^+(aq) + OH^−(aq) → NH3(aq) + H2O(ℓ).

prompt: What happens once one of a buffer's two solutes has completely reacted with added acid or base?

choices.text: The solution is no longer a buffer, and rapid changes in pH may occur.
The buffer keeps working forever.
choices.why: Buffers work only for limited amounts of added acid or base; they have a certain capacity.

choices.text: The solution becomes neutral.
choices.why: Once one solute is used up, more acid or base can change the pH rapidly, in either direction.

choices.text: The other solute takes over both jobs.
choices.why: Each solute handles only one direction. With one gone, the solution can no longer resist pH changes both ways.

explanation: Buffers work well only for limited amounts of added strong acid or base. Once either solute is completely reacted, the solution is no longer a buffer: a buffer has a certain capacity.

prompt: Which buffer has the larger capacity?

choices.text: One with more of its two solutes dissolved in it
One with less of its two solutes dissolved in it
choices.why: Less solute is used up sooner by added acid or base, so its capacity is smaller.

choices.text: One made with a strong acid
choices.why: Strong acids can't make buffers at all.

choices.text: All buffers have the same capacity.
choices.why: Capacity depends on how much solute the buffer has to react with added acid or base.

explanation: Buffers that have more initial solute dissolved in them have larger capacities: they can react with more added acid or base before a solute runs out.

prompt: Without a correcting mechanism, why would a small amount of stomach acid entering the bloodstream be dangerous?

choices.text: Very small amounts of strong acid can change the pH of a solution very quickly.
Stomach acid is a weak acid that ionizes slowly.
choices.why: Stomach acid (approximated as HCl) is a strong acid; that's why even a little would change the pH quickly.

choices.text: Stomach acid would make the blood basic.
choices.why: An acid would lower the blood's pH, making it more acidic.

choices.text: Blood can't contain any H^+ ions.
choices.why: Blood does contain H^+ (its pH is about 7.4); the danger is a sharp change.

explanation: Strong acids produce a relatively large amount of H^+, and very small amounts can change pH quickly. 1 mL of stomach acid added to the bloodstream with no correcting mechanism would drop the blood's pH from about 7.4 to about 4.7.

prompt: Without buffering, adding 1 mL of stomach acid to the bloodstream would drop the blood's pH from about 7.4 to about 4.7. By how many pH units would it fall?
If the blood's pH fell from 7.4 to 4.7, by what factor would [H^+] increase?
explanation: Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so a drop of 2.7 units multiplies [H^+] by 10^2.7 = 5.0 × 10^2, about 500 times.

prompt: One buffer in human blood is based on which pair of species?

choices.text: HCO3^− and H2CO3
HCl and NaCl
choices.why: HCl is a strong acid, so HCl and NaCl can't buffer anything.

choices.text: NaOH and NaCl
choices.why: NaOH is a strong base; this pair isn't a buffer.

choices.text: H2O and O2
choices.why: Blood's buffer is based on HCO3^− and H2CO3, a weak acid and its anion.

explanation: One buffer in blood is based on HCO3^− and H2CO3 (another way to write CO2(aq)). With it present, even stomach acid reaching the bloodstream would change the blood's pH only minimally.

prompt: In the blood's HCO3^−/H2CO3 buffer, what is H2CO3 another way of writing?

choices.text: CO2(aq)
HCO3^−
choices.why: HCO3^− is the other member of the pair, with one fewer H^+.

choices.text: H2O
choices.why: H2CO3 contains carbon; it is another way to write dissolved CO2.
CO3^2− has two fewer protons. H2CO3 is CO2(aq).

explanation: In the blood buffer based on HCO3^− and H2CO3, the second compound is another way to write CO2(aq).

prompt: Inside many of the body's cells, the buffering system is based on which ions?

choices.text: Phosphate ions
Chloride ions
choices.why: Cl^− comes from a strong acid and can't buffer. The section names phosphate ions.

choices.text: Sodium ions
choices.why: Na^+ comes from a strong base and doesn't affect pH. Cells use phosphate buffers.

choices.text: Hydronium ions only
choices.why: A buffer needs a pair of species that can take up both acid and base; inside cells it is based on phosphate ions.

explanation: Inside many of the body's cells, there is a buffering system based on phosphate ions; in the blood, one buffer is based on HCO3^− and H2CO3.

prompt: Aspirin, acetylsalicylic acid, isn't on the list of strong acids. Why can it still cause problems in the stomach?

choices.text: It is a weak acid, but still an acid, and some people take relatively large amounts daily.
It is a strong base.
choices.why: Aspirin is an acid: the H atom in its CO2H group can be donated.

choices.text: Weak acids are more dangerous than strong ones.
choices.why: That's not the point. Aspirin is a weak acid, but large daily amounts of any acid can irritate the stomach lining.

choices.text: It turns into stomach acid, HCl.
choices.why: Aspirin stays acetylsalicylic acid; its own acidic nature is the problem.

explanation: Acetylsalicylic acid acts as a Brønsted-Lowry acid and, not being a strong acid, is weak. It is still an acid, though, and its acidic nature can cause problems in the stomach lining for people who take a lot of it.

prompt: Buffered aspirin contains a buffering agent to minimize aspirin's acidic side effects. What is that agent usually?

choices.text: MgO
HCl
choices.why: HCl is stomach acid itself; adding it would make things worse.

choices.text: NaCl
choices.why: NaCl is a neutral salt and doesn't regulate acidity.

choices.text: H2SO4
choices.why: H2SO4 is a strong acid, the opposite of what's needed.

explanation: Buffered aspirin also contains a buffering agent, usually MgO, that regulates the acidity of the aspirin to minimize its acidic side effects.

prompt: Why does the pH of an acetate buffer barely change when a little NaOH is added?

choices.text: The added OH^− reacts with HC2H3O2 to form water, so little free OH^− remains.
NaOH doesn't dissolve in a buffer.
choices.why: NaOH dissolves and releases OH^−; the buffer's weak acid then reacts with it.

choices.text: The buffer makes NaOH a weak base.
choices.why: NaOH stays a strong base. Its OH^− is consumed by HC2H3O2.

choices.text: The buffer's pH is fixed at 7 no matter what.
choices.why: Buffers resist pH changes; they don't fix the pH at 7.

explanation: Rather than changing the pH dramatically, the added OH^− ions react with HC2H3O2 to make H2O and C2H3O2^−, so the pH does not change much.

prompt: A buffer contains 0.10 mol of HC2H3O2 and 0.10 mol of NaC2H3O2. What is the most NaOH, in moles, that the buffer can neutralize before its HC2H3O2 is used up?
explanation: Each OH^− reacts with one HC2H3O2: HC2H3O2 + OH^− → H2O + C2H3O2^−. 0.10 mol of HC2H3O2 can neutralize 0.10 mol of NaOH; after that, the solution is no longer a buffer.

prompt: A buffer contains 0.10 mol of HC2H3O2 and 0.10 mol of C2H3O2^−. 0.020 mol of NaOH is added. How many moles of C2H3O2^− are present afterward?
explanation: HC2H3O2 + OH^− → H2O + C2H3O2^−: the 0.020 mol of OH^− turns 0.020 mol of HC2H3O2 into C2H3O2^−, giving 0.10 + 0.020 = 0.12 mol of C2H3O2^−.

prompt: A buffer contains 0.10 mol of HC2H3O2 and 0.10 mol of C2H3O2^−. 0.030 mol of HCl is added. How many moles of HC2H3O2 are present afterward?
explanation: H^+ + C2H3O2^− → HC2H3O2: the 0.030 mol of H^+ turns 0.030 mol of C2H3O2^− into HC2H3O2, giving 0.10 + 0.030 = 0.13 mol of HC2H3O2.
